newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuba clears up after Lili, says crop losses heavy.
newsitem.headline: Cuba clears up after Lili, says crop losses heavy.

text.p: Hurricane Lili caused big losses to Cuba's farm produce and hundreds of workers were busy repairing damaged homes and factories, downed power lines and salvaging ravaged crops, officials said on Sunday.

Agriculture Minister Alfredo Jordan said banana and citrus plantations had been particularly hard hit by Lili's erratic path on Thursday night and on Friday across the island's western and central provinces.

"We're working to recover everything that can still be used," Jordan told Cuban news agency Prensa Latina during a tour to inspect crop damage in the provinces of Pinar del Rio, Havana, Matanzas, Sancti Spiritus, Villa Clara and Cienfuegos.
Large areas of sugar cane, Cuba's main export crop, were also reported to have been either flooded or flattened by the torrential rains and winds gusting up to 110 mph (180 kph) carried by Lili.

A fall in hard currency farm exports would represent a major blow to Cuba's cash-strapped economy, which was still fighting to recover from a five-year recession caused by the collapse of trade and aid ties with the former Soviet bloc.

Whole plantations of bananas, an important staple in the daily diet of ordinary Cubans, were devastated by the storm. State radio quoted agriculture officials as saying 46 percent of the nation's banana production was hit by the hurricane.
Brigades of workers and soldiers rushed to salvage banana bunches so they could be rapidly transported to markets.

Jordan said the level of losses at Cuba's main citrus growing areas, the Isle of Youth and Jaguey Grande in Matanzas province, meant the island would not now be able to achieve the planned production target for this year of 700,000 tons.
"Practically 100 percent of mature fruits and those at other stages of ripeness fell," Prensa Latina quoted Jordan as saying. The ground beneath the trees was blanketed with fruit.

Losses of grapefruit and oranges, some of which were destined for export, were estimated by the state media at 15,000 tons on the Isle of Youth and 120,000 tons at Jaguey Grande. There were also heavy losses in Cienfuegos province.

The full extent of damage to sugar cane fields was not yet clear. State television said large areas affected had just a month or so remaining before the start of the 1996-97 harvest in which Cuba hopes to lift sugar production above five million tons, from 4.45 million this year. Sugar mills and warehouses also suffered damage, especially to their roofs.

Jordan said hundreds of seed beds and nurseries of tobacco plants were destroyed, which would set back Cuba's efforts to increase its crop of the high-quality tobacco that goes into making world-famous Havana cigars.

Ricefields in Pinar del Rio and Sancti Spiritus provinces had also been hit by flooding while hundreds of workers were being mobilized across the island to pick the coffee crop that was threatened by over-ripening because of the high humidity.
The province that received the worst impact of the hurricane was Cienfuegos, where factories, hospitals and 10,000 homes were damaged -- 2,000 of the homes completely.

The whole province was still without electricity on Sunday because a local thermoelectric power station was out of service. Most of neighboring Villa Clara province also had no power while Matanzas and Sancti Spiritus had only half of their electricity grids working. Officials said it would take up to 20 days to restore the situation to normal.
Schools were scheduled to reopen on Monday.

Despite the damage, Cuban authorities were congratulating themselves that Lili did not claim a single life, largely due to a well-organized civil defense operation that quickly evacuated more than 200,000 people both before and after the hurricane slammed into the southwest coast on Thursday night.
